en_title: Couple Relationships in the New Era
en_excerpt: What are couple relationships for today, now that surviving together is no longer the point?
en_meta_description: Why the purpose of relationships is shifting from surviving together to living with awareness — and what that asks of couples today.
en_content:
When the purpose stops being about surviving together and becomes about living with awareness

Text: Juliana Gomes

Founder of Escola Mulher Sistêmica

Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/juliana.mendes.gomes/

https://mulhersistemica.my.canva.site/adultecer-para-amar

We are in the week of Valentine's Day.

A time when shop windows fill up with hearts, social media floods with declarations of love and, inevitably, we are invited to reflect on our relationships.

But perhaps the most important question is not whether we are loving or being loved.

Perhaps the question is:

What are couple relationships for in the times we live in?

This is a question that has run through my work with women over the last few years. And the more I observe their stories, their challenges and their processes of transformation, the more I see that we are living through a profound change in the way we understand love, partnership and life as a couple.

For thousands of years, relationships had a very clear function: to guarantee the continuity of life.

Our ancestors joined together in order to survive.

Marriages were, above all, structures that sustained the family, the household economy, protection and reproduction. Love could exist, but it was not necessarily the centre of the choice.

Survival was.

It was through this model that life reached us.

And it is important to acknowledge that with respect.

Life crossed wars, scarcity, illness, losses, inequalities and countless challenges in order to keep existing. Our parents, grandparents and great-grandparents carried burdens we often cannot even imagine.

That is why we also inherited deep beliefs about relationships.

The idea that loving requires sacrifice.

The idea that we must endure.

The idea that individual happiness must be put second in order to preserve the family.

The idea that staying is always better than leaving.

But something is changing.

For the first time in history, millions of people are asking themselves not only how to survive, but how to live.

The search for therapy, self-knowledge, spirituality, personal development and emotional health has never been so intense.

People want to understand who they are.

They want to discover their purposes.

They want to find meaning.

And when individuals change, relationships inevitably change too.

Perhaps that is why we see so many questions arising.

Couples who choose not to have children.

Women who decide to postpone motherhood.

New family configurations.

Separations that once seemed unthinkable.

People seeking different ways of building a shared life.

I do not believe we are witnessing the end of love.

I believe we are witnessing the end of a model of relationship that no longer answers the needs of a new consciousness.

The data reinforce this perception.

Brazil has been recording record numbers of divorces, and a significant share of those separations happens before even ten years of relationship.

But perhaps the question is not why relationships are ending.

Perhaps the question is: what did they come to teach us?

In my experience, couple relationships remain one of the greatest paths of self-knowledge available to a human being.

It is in the encounter with the other that our wounds appear.

It is in the everydayness of living together that our needs, fears, expectations and unconscious patterns reveal themselves.

The other becomes a mirror.

And we do not always like what we see reflected.

Perhaps that is why so many women begin their therapeutic processes motivated by relational pain.

Many arrive hoping to save a relationship.

But they end up finding themselves.

They discover that some questions are not about the partner.

They are about them.

About their limits.

About their self-esteem.

About their family history.

About the way they learned to love.

About what they believe they deserve.

And here one of the greatest challenges of contemporary relationships arises.

What happens when one person grows and the other stays in the same place?

What happens when a woman begins to expand her awareness, look at her pain, review her beliefs and build a new relationship with herself?

This is a delicate question, but a necessary one.

Because relationships are not made up of love alone.

They are made up of exchanges.

Of shared responsibility.

Of common purpose.

Of willingness to grow.

No relationship can evolve beyond the level of consciousness of the people who make it up.

Perhaps that is why New Era relationships demand something that was not so necessary before: deep conversations about purpose.

Not only about children.

Not only about money.

Not only about where to live or which goals to reach.

But about who we are becoming.

About which life we want to build.

About which values we wish to sustain.

About which consciousness we want to cultivate together.

I believe the new purpose of couple relationships is not only to guarantee that life continues.

I believe it is to help life flourish.

To create spaces where two people can grow, mature, awaken and expand their consciousness without having to abandon themselves in order to stay together.

Perhaps our ancestors joined together to guarantee the survival of life.

Perhaps our generation is being invited to learn something different.

To learn to live this life with more truth.

More presence.

More freedom.

And more awareness.

Because, in the end, perhaps New Era love is not about finding someone who completes us.

Perhaps it is about finding someone willing to walk beside us while both of us keep transforming.
